title: Offers and verticals
summary: A deep look at the verticals operators actually run: trading, iGaming, finance, sweepstakes and e-commerce, with the regulation, qualification rules and payout maths behind each. lessons.title: Trading offers in depth
objectives: By the end you can explain how a trading offer pays, from click to qualified FTD.

steps.h: What a trading offer really pays for
steps.p: A trading offer pays you when someone you referred opens a broker account, passes identity checks and makes a first deposit that meets the broker's rules. You are sending adults to a leveraged, high-risk product. Your job is to send people who understand that, not people sold a dream.
steps.more: Brokers in many regulated markets must publish the share of retail accounts that lose money on leveraged products, and in the EU and UK that share is typically a clear majority. Keep that in mind when you write any ad. Your traffic is only worth something if the person stays, deposits again and trades. Users who were promised easy money leave fast, complain, and get offers pulled from networks.

d.s: You send informed adults, not dreamers

steps.say: Let's start with what a trading offer actually pays for. You get paid when someone you referred opens a broker account, passes identity checks, and makes a first deposit that meets the broker's rules. Notice the words on screen: a regulated, high-risk product. You're sending adults to leveraged trading. In the E U and U K, brokers often publish that a clear majority of retail accounts lose money. So your job is to send informed adults, not people sold a dream, because people promised easy money leave fast, complain, and get offers pulled.

steps.h: The product types you will meet
steps.p: Trading offers are not all the same. The product decides the regulation, the audience and what you are allowed to say. Read the offer page to see exactly what the broker sells before you plan a single ad.
d: Forex and CFDs|leveraged, high risk, licensed by country
Fixed-time or digital options|banned or restricted in many places
Stocks and ETFs apps|lower leverage, still capital at risk
Crypto exchanges|rules vary fast by country
Copy trading|someone else trades, risk is still yours
steps.more: Fixed-time, binary or digital options are banned for retail clients in many countries and are not allowed on most ad platforms at the time of writing. Steer away from them as a beginner, even when a network shows a high payout. Check the current ad policy and the regulator in your geo before you consider any trading product.
steps.say: Trading offers are not all the same. Look at these five cards. Forex and C F Ds are leveraged and licensed by country. Fixed-time or digital options are banned or restricted in many places, so steer away from them as a beginner, even when the payout looks high. Stock and E T F apps have lower leverage, but capital is still at risk. Crypto exchange rules change fast by country. And with copy trading, someone else trades, but the risk is still yours. Always read the offer page and check the current ad policy and regulator in your geo first.

steps.p: Each step loses people and each step can take time. The broker only pays your network once the last step is confirmed, and your network then pays you on its own schedule.
steps.say: Here's the journey from click to a paid F T D, which means first time deposit. Follow the flow from left to right: click, registration, the K Y C identity check, the first deposit, the baseline being met, and finally a paid F T D. Every step loses people, and every step can take time. The broker only pays your network once that last step is confirmed, and then your network pays you on its own schedule. So money always arrives later than the click.

steps.h: Words on every trading offer page
steps.p: These five terms decide what you are paid for. If an offer page does not define them clearly, ask your affiliate manager in writing before you send a single click.

rows: This is what you get paid

steps.say: These five terms appear on almost every trading offer page, and they decide what you're paid for. Reg means an account was created, and it's rarely paid alone. K Y C means the person's I D and address were checked. F T D is the first deposit, usually with a minimum amount. The baseline is the set of rules an F T D must meet. And Q F T D, a qualified F T D, is the one that met the baseline. That's what you get paid for. If any term is vague, ask your affiliate manager in writing.

steps.p: The baseline is the set of conditions that turns a raw deposit into a paid one. Brokers use it to avoid paying for tiny or fake deposits. Every network writes it differently, so read the exact wording.
d: Minimum first deposit, for example $10 or $50
Minimum number of trades or volume
A time window, for example within 30 days
One account per person and device
Allowed geos and traffic sources only
steps.say: The baseline is what turns a raw deposit into a paid one. Brokers use it so they don't pay for tiny or fake deposits. steps.h: Raw FTDs are not paid FTDs
steps.p: Example: your tracker shows 50 FTDs this week, but only 32 met the baseline. That is a 64% qualification rate. You are paid for 32, not 50, so plan on the smaller number.
steps.say: Here's a trap that catches many beginners. In this example, your tracker shows fifty F T Ds this week, but only thirty two met the baseline. That's a sixty four percent qualification rate. Follow the equation on screen: fifty raw F T Ds, times sixty four percent, equals thirty two paid. You're paid for thirty two, not fifty. So always plan your numbers on the smaller figure, the one that actually gets paid.

steps.h: What a raw FTD is really worth
steps.p: Example: the offer pays $40 per qualified FTD and 64% of your raw FTDs qualify. Multiply them and each raw FTD in your tracker is worth $25.60. Bid against this number, not against the headline $40.
steps.more: Worked example. $40 × 0.64 = $25.60. If you judged the campaign at $40 per raw FTD, a cost per raw FTD of $30 would look like a $10 profit. In reality you would lose $4.40 on every raw FTD ($25.60 − $30). The qualification rate changes by geo, creative and audience, so track it per campaign and update it every week.
steps.say: So what's one raw F T D in your tracker really worth? In this example, the offer pays forty dollars per qualified F T D, and sixty four percent qualify. Forty times nought point six four gives twenty five dollars and sixty cents. That's the big number on screen. Here's why it matters. If you paid thirty dollars per raw F T D thinking each was worth forty, you'd think you made ten dollars profit. In reality you'd lose four dollars forty on each one. The rate changes by geo, creative and audience, so track it weekly per campaign.

steps.h: A trading funnel with real drop-off
steps.p: Example: 1,000 clicks from a test. 180 registered, 36 deposited and 24 met the baseline. Every stage loses people, and the biggest lost money hides between FTD and qualified FTD.
steps.say: Now look at a whole trading funnel with real drop-off. In this example, a test sends one thousand clicks. One hundred and eighty people register, thirty six deposit, and twenty four meet the baseline. See how each bar shrinks. Every stage loses people, but notice the step between raw F T D and qualified F T D. That's where the lost money hides, because those twelve deposits looked like wins in your tracker but were never paid.

steps.p: Example: you spent $720 on those 1,000 clicks. Priced on raw FTDs the test looks strong. Priced on qualified FTDs it is still profitable, but with far less room for error.
steps.more: Revenue is 24 qualified × $40 = $960. Profit is $960 − $720 = $240, which is a 33% ROI ($240 ÷ $720). Cost per raw FTD is $720 ÷ 36 = $20. Cost per qualified FTD is $720 ÷ 24 = $30. If you scale while watching only the $20 figure, a small drop in qualification rate can wipe out the margin without you noticing.
steps.say: Here's the same test, priced two ways. You spent seven hundred and twenty dollars. In the raw view, thirty six F T Ds cost twenty dollars each, which looks strong. In the qualified view, twenty four F T Ds cost thirty dollars each. Revenue is twenty four times forty, nine hundred and sixty dollars, so profit is two hundred and forty dollars, about a thirty three percent R O I, return on investment. Still profitable, but with much less room for error. Watch only the twenty dollar figure, and a small drop in qualification could wipe out your margin unnoticed.

steps.p: Example: share of a week's final FTDs and qualified FTDs that have been reported, by day after the click. Many deposits and most qualifications land days later, so early numbers always look worse than the truth.
steps.say: Conversions arrive late, and this curve shows why that matters. In this example, the top line shows F T Ds reported as a share of the final total, and the lower line shows qualified F T Ds. On day one, only about half the F T Ds and a fifth of the qualified ones have shown up. Even by day seven, qualified F T Ds are still at eighty percent. So early numbers always look worse than the truth. Don't panic on day one.

steps.h: Starting rules for a trading test
steps.p: Example: target $30 per qualified FTD, payout $40, so break-even is $40. Use network-confirmed qualified FTDs, and only once postbacks for that spend have had time to arrive. These are starting rules; adapt them to your offer and data.
steps.more: Why the kill line here is $40 and not $45: 1.5 × $30 is $45, but the offer only pays $40, so every QFTD above $40 loses money. The card always uses the lower of the two. Why wait for matured data: the curve on the last slide shows qualified FTDs still arriving a week later. Judge the zero-conversion rule only on spend whose postbacks have had time to land. Full rule card and timing: Budget and kill rules module.

rows: Spend ≥ 3 × target, CPA above lower of 1.5 × target and break-even
≥ 3 conversions, CPA ≤ 0.8 × target, ≥ 48 h since last step

steps.say: These are starting rules for a trading test. In the example, your target is thirty dollars per qualified F T D, and the payout is forty, so break-even is forty. Read the table row by row. Kill if you've spent two times target, sixty dollars, with zero conversions. Kill if you've spent three times target and C P A, cost per acquisition, is above forty. Notice the kill line is forty, not forty five, because above forty you lose money. Scale by twenty percent with three or more conversions at twenty four dollars or less, forty eight hours after the last step. Otherwise, hold. Only judge matured, network-confirmed data, and adapt these to your offer.

steps.h: Licences and platform rules come first
steps.p: Before any spend, confirm the broker is licensed or allowed to serve the country you target, the network approves your traffic source, and the ad platform allows financial products there. At the time of writing many platforms require extra verification for financial ads; check the current policy. Get all three in writing.
steps.more: Regulators differ by country. Examples include the SEC in Nigeria, the Capital Markets Authority in Kenya and the FSCA in South Africa. A broker licensed offshore may still be unwelcome in your target country. Rules change, so check the regulator's own website and the current ad policy every time you open a new geo. steps.p: Your ad and lander set the user's expectations. Honest messaging attracts people who stay and trade. Income promises attract people who leave, complain and get your account restricted.

Judging the test on day one

steps.say: Finally, here's your checklist before running any trading offer. Run it for every new offer and every new geo. The broker can legally serve the geo. The conditions a first deposit must meet to be paid, such as a minimum amount, a number of trades and a time window.

quiz.q: An offer pays $50 per qualified FTD. 70% of your raw FTDs qualify. What is one raw FTD worth?
quiz.why: $50 × 0.70 = $35. The headline payout only applies to FTDs that meet the baseline.

quiz.why: 2 × $30 = $60. $65 spent with zero network-confirmed conversions on matured data meets the zero-conversion kill rule.

steps.h: Price the CPA you will actually receive
steps.p: Example: the offer pays $50 CPA. Of 80 raw FTDs, 60 met the deposit and wagering baseline, a 75% rate. Each raw FTD in your tracker is worth $37.50 before any profit.
steps.say: Now price the C P A you'll actually receive. In this example, the offer pays fifty dollars. Of eighty raw F T Ds, sixty met the deposit and wagering baseline. That's a seventy five percent rate. Follow the equation: fifty dollars, times seventy five percent, equals thirty seven dollars fifty per raw F T D. That's what each deposit in your tracker is worth, before any profit.

steps.h: Your maximum cost per raw FTD
steps.p: Example: you want a 25% margin on revenue. Keep 25% of $37.50 and the most you can pay per raw FTD is $28.13. Above that, you are either breaking even or losing money.
steps.more: Worked example. 80 raw FTDs × $37.50 = $3,000 expected revenue, which matches 60 qualified × $50. A 25% margin on revenue means cost can be at most 75% of revenue: $37.50 × 0.75 = $28.125, rounded to $28.13. If your test shows $26 per raw FTD you have room. At $32 you lose margin and must improve creative, audience or funnel before scaling.
steps.say: Next, your maximum cost per raw F T D. In this example you want a twenty five percent margin on revenue, so cost can be at most seventy five percent of value. Thirty seven fifty times nought point seven five gives twenty eight dollars and thirteen cents, the number on screen. Above that, you're breaking even or losing money. So if your test shows twenty six dollars per raw F T D, you have room. At thirty two dollars, you need to improve creative, audience or funnel before you scale.

lessons.title: RevShare and hybrid maths
objectives: By the end you can calculate RevShare earnings from NGR for a cohort of players.
You can compare CPA, RevShare and hybrid deals over the same period.

steps.h: RevShare pays a share of what the player is worth
steps.p: With RevShare you earn a percentage of the net revenue the operator makes from players you referred, usually every month for as long as the deal lasts. You trade a fixed payment today for a share of an uncertain future.
steps.say: With RevShare, you earn a percentage of the net revenue the operator makes from players you referred, usually every month for as long as the deal lasts. Notice the words on screen: a share of future revenue, paid monthly, never guaranteed. You're trading a fixed payment today for a share of an uncertain future. That trade is what this whole lesson is about.

steps.p: In iGaming, RevShare is usually paid on Net Gaming Revenue, or NGR. Each operator defines it in its terms, so read exactly which costs are removed before your percentage is applied.
steps.say: In iGaming, RevShare is usually paid on N G R, net gaming revenue. Follow the flow. Start with what players bet, minus what they win. That gives G G R, gross gaming revenue. Then the operator removes bonuses, fees and taxes. What's left is N G R, and your percentage is applied to that. Each operator defines N G R in its own terms, so read exactly which costs are removed before your share is calculated.

steps.p: Example: a player bets and loses $60 net in a month, so GGR is $60. The operator removes $10 in bonuses and $8 in fees and taxes, leaving $42 NGR. At 30% RevShare you earn $12.60 that month.
steps.say: Let's do one player for one month. In this example, a player bets and loses sixty dollars net, so G G R is sixty dollars. The operator removes ten dollars in bonuses and eight dollars in fees and taxes, which leaves forty two dollars N G R. Follow the equation: forty two dollars, times thirty percent RevShare, equals twelve dollars sixty. That's your earning from that player that month.

steps.h: A cohort of 100 FTDs over seven months
steps.p: Example: 100 players who all deposited in the same month. Their combined NGR falls each month as players drift away. At 35% RevShare, this is what you earn month by month.
steps.more: Worked example. NGR by month: $3,000, $1,800, $1,200, $900, $700, $600, $500. Total $8,700. Your 35% share: $1,050, $630, $420, $315, $245, $210, $175, which adds up to $3,045. Per FTD that is $3,045 ÷ 100 = $30.45 over seven months. The shape matters as much as the total: more than a third of all earnings arrive in month one.
steps.say: Now a whole cohort. In this example, one hundred players all deposited in the same month. Read down the table. Their combined N G R starts at three thousand dollars in month one, then falls as players drift away, down to five hundred by month seven. At thirty five percent, you earn one thousand and fifty in month one, and the running total reaches three thousand and forty five dollars. That's about thirty dollars forty five per F T D, or first time deposit. Notice that more than a third of everything arrives in month one.

steps.p: Example: the same 100 FTDs on a $25 CPA pay $2,500 once. On 35% RevShare the running total passes $2,500 in month five. Before that point CPA was ahead.
steps.say: When does RevShare overtake C P A? In this example, the same hundred F T Ds on a twenty five dollar C P A, cost per acquisition, pay two thousand five hundred dollars once. That's the flat line. The rising line is the RevShare running total. Follow it, and you'll see it passes two thousand five hundred in month five. Before that point, C P A was ahead. So a fair comparison always looks across months, not just the first one.

steps.p: Example: a hybrid pays $15 CPA per qualified FTD plus 20% RevShare. On the same cohort that is $1,500 upfront plus 20% of $8,700, which is $1,740, for a total of $3,240.
steps.say: A hybrid deal mixes both. In this example, the deal pays fifteen dollars C P A per qualified F T D, plus twenty percent RevShare. On the same cohort, that's one thousand five hundred dollars upfront, plus twenty percent of eight thousand seven hundred, which is one thousand seven hundred and forty. Follow the equation: a total of three thousand two hundred and forty dollars. You get some cash quickly, and still share in the future.

steps.h: Three deals on the same 100 FTDs
steps.p: Example: over seven months, the hybrid earns the most, RevShare is close behind and CPA earns least. With a weaker cohort the order can flip, so this is a comparison method, not a rule.
steps.say: Here are three deals on the same hundred F T Ds over seven months. Look at the bars. The twenty five dollar C P A earns two thousand five hundred. Thirty five percent RevShare earns three thousand and forty five. And the hybrid earns the most, three thousand two hundred and forty. But this is an example. With a weaker cohort the order can flip. So treat this as a method for comparing deals, not a rule about which one wins.

steps.p: Some deals carry negative months forward. If your players win big, NGR goes below zero and that loss is deducted from future earnings. Check whether your deal carries negatives forward or resets them each month.
steps.more: Worked example at 35%. Month A: one player wins big and cohort NGR is −$500, so your share is −$175. With carryover you get $0 and owe −$175 against the future. Month B: NGR is $1,000, your share is $350, minus $175 carried, so you are paid $175. Without carryover you would have been paid $0 in month A and $350 in month B. Many affiliates ask for no negative carryover; whether you get it depends on your volume and the operator.

d.text: Example: −$175 carried forward turns a $350 month into a $175 payment.

steps.say: Some deals carry negative months forward. If your players win big, N G R goes below zero, and that loss is taken from future earnings. Here's the example on screen, at thirty five percent. One month, N G R is minus five hundred, so your share is minus one hundred and seventy five. Next month your share is three hundred and fifty, but the carried loss is deducted, so you're paid one hundred and seventy five. Many affiliates ask for no negative carryover. Whether you get it depends on your volume and the operator. Always check.

steps.p: Example: you paid $22 per FTD in ads. On the RevShare cohort above, each FTD returns $10.50 in month one, $16.80 by month two, $21 by month three and $24.15 by month four. You only get your ad money back in month four.
steps.more: This gap is the real cost of RevShare. You pay for ads today, often with a card or a credit line, and wait months to recover it. With CPA at $25 you would have earned $3 margin per FTD on normal net terms. RevShare can be worth more in the end, but only if you can fund the wait and the operator keeps paying. Many operators start new affiliates on CPA or hybrid for exactly this reason.

steps.p: There is no best deal, only the deal that fits your cash, your data and your risk tolerance. Most operators start on CPA and move part of their volume to hybrid once they trust the player quality.

On the right, RevShare or hybrid fits when you have cash to wait, you've seen cohort data, players redeposit for months, and the operator is stable and trusted. Most operators start on C P A and move part of their volume to hybrid once they trust the quality.

steps.h: Never push players to lose more
steps.p: Your RevShare grows when players lose, which creates a pull towards harmful marketing. Never encourage chasing losses, bigger deposits or 'win it back' messages. Operators and regulators treat that as harmful marketing and can end your deal.

steps.p: The paid event decides how long you wait for data and how much fraud risk you carry. The later the event in the funnel, the more each conversion is worth and the fewer you will see.

steps.say: Now sweepstakes. These offers pay when a person enters a prize draw and agrees to receive marketing. Double opt-in, D O I, pays only after they confirm by email or S M S. It's two steps, a higher payout and better quality, but fewer conversions. D O I pays more per lead precisely because fewer people complete it.

steps.p: The classic sweepstakes violation is telling someone they have won, or showing a fake countdown. Say they can enter a draw for a chance to win, and link to the official rules. Anything else is misleading.

steps.h: What a placed order is worth
steps.p: Example: payout is $8 per delivered order. 105 of 200 placed orders were delivered, a 52.5% rate. Each order on your dashboard is worth $4.20, not $8.
steps.more: Worked example. Revenue is 105 × $8 = $840. You spent $600 for 200 orders, a cost per order of $3. Cost per delivered order is $600 ÷ 105 = $5.71. Profit is $840 − $600 = $240, a 40% ROI. If confirmation drops to 60% and delivery to 70%, only 84 orders pay, revenue falls to $672 and profit to $72. Track confirmation and delivery rates as closely as you track CPA.
steps.say: So what's a placed order really worth? In this example, the payout is eight dollars per delivered order, and one hundred and five of two hundred orders were delivered. That's a fifty two point five percent rate. Follow the equation: eight dollars, times fifty two point five percent, equals four dollars twenty per order. Not eight. If you spent six hundred dollars on those two hundred orders, revenue is eight hundred and forty, and profit is two hundred and forty. Track confirmation and delivery rates as closely as you track C P A, your cost per acquisition.

steps.p: On COD and loan offers the paid event arrives days later. Set your target on the paid event, judge the kill rules only on spend old enough for deliveries or approvals to land, and use orders as an early signal, not a verdict. Starting rules; adapt them.

An ad set at $4 per placed order is heading for about $7.62 per delivered order, above target, so it goes on Hold until real deliveries confirm it. Full rule card: Budget and kill rules module.

objectives: By the end you can score an offer on more than its payout.

steps.h: The payout is the least important number
steps.p: New buyers pick the offer with the biggest payout. Operators pick the offer that pays most per dollar of traffic, pays on time and keeps paying. A $60 offer that scrubs half your FTDs is worse than a clean $40 offer.
steps.say: Here's a surprising idea: the payout is the least important number. New buyers pick the biggest payout. Operators pick the offer that pays most per dollar of traffic, pays on time, and keeps paying. As the screen says, value per click beats payout, and paid beats promised. A sixty dollar offer that scrubs half your F T Ds, first time deposits, is worse than a clean forty dollar offer.

steps.p: Score each offer from 1 to 5 on these lines before you test it. Write the scores down. After the test, compare your guesses with real results and you will get better at choosing.

steps.say: Before you test any offer, score it from one to five on each line of this scorecard. Payout and baseline: what's a raw F T D really worth? Conversion rate: do clicks become deposits in your geo? Legality and approval: is it licensed and allowed on your source? Payment terms: how often and how reliably are you paid? Caps: can it take your planned volume? Support: does the manager answer and help? Write the scores down. After the test, compare your guesses with real results, and you'll get better at choosing.

steps.p: EPC, earnings per click, puts offers with different payouts on the same scale. Example: Offer A pays $60 but converts 1 in 200 clicks. Offer B pays $40 and converts 1 in 100. B earns more per click.
steps.more: Worked example. Offer A: $60 × (1 ÷ 200) = $0.30 EPC. Offer B: $40 × (1 ÷ 100) = $0.40 EPC. If your clicks cost $0.32, Offer A loses $0.02 per click while Offer B makes $0.08. Use qualified conversions in this calculation, and use your own geo and traffic source, because a network's average EPC mixes everyone's traffic.
steps.say: E P C, earnings per click, puts offers with different payouts on the same scale. The formula on screen is payout times qualified conversions per click. In this example, offer A pays sixty dollars but converts one in two hundred clicks. That's thirty cents per click. Offer B pays forty dollars and converts one in one hundred. That's forty cents. So B earns more per click. Use qualified conversions, and use your own geo and traffic, because a network's average E P C mixes everyone's traffic.

steps.p: These four terms decide when and whether you get paid. They are often more important than the payout, so get each one in writing before you scale.
d: Cap|max conversions paid per day or month
Hold|days before a conversion is approved
Net terms|days from period end to payment, for example Net 15
Minimum payout|balance needed before you are paid
steps.say: These four terms decide when, and whether, you get paid. Look at the cards. A cap is the maximum conversions paid per day or month. A hold is the number of days before a conversion is approved. Net terms are the days from the end of the period to payment, for example net fifteen. And the minimum payout is the balance you need before you're paid. These often matter more than the payout itself, so get each one in writing before you scale.

steps.p: If an offer has a cap of 20 FTDs a day and you send 30, the extra 10 are usually not paid. Ask for the cap, set a daily alert, and pause or redirect spend when you are close.
steps.more: Example: payout $40, cost per FTD $28. At 20 FTDs you earn $800 and spend $560, profit $240. Send 30 FTDs and you spend $840 but are still paid $800, so profit becomes −$40. A busy day above cap can wipe out the whole day's profit. Ask your manager whether a cap can be raised before you scale, not after.

d.text: Example: 30 FTDs sent on a 20 cap. Spend $840, paid $800. Loss $40.

steps.say: Over-cap traffic is unpaid traffic. If an offer has a cap of twenty F T Ds a day and you send thirty, the extra ten are usually not paid. Here's the example on screen. Payout forty dollars, cost per F T D twenty eight. You send thirty, so you spend eight hundred and forty dollars, but you're only paid eight hundred. That's a forty dollar loss on a busy day. Ask for the cap, set a daily alert, and pause or redirect spend when you're close.

steps.h: How to ask for a higher payout
steps.p: Payout increases are earned with data and consistency, not by asking on day one. Managers can only push for more if you give them numbers they can show the advertiser.
steps.say: Payout increases are earned with data and consistency, not by asking on day one. Follow the flow. Run clean volume. Share quality data. Show steady growth. Ask with a specific number. And agree it in writing. Managers can only push for more if you give them numbers they can show the advertiser.

steps.h: Asking for a raise, in practice
steps.p: Example of a payout conversation in a Telegram-style chat with an affiliate manager. The buyer leads with data, asks for a specific number and confirms in writing. No threats, no bluff.

messages.text: Hi Grace. Last 6 weeks on offer 4821 in KE: 118 QFTDs a month, 71% qualification, under 2% chargebacks. Sub ID report attached.
Thanks, the advertiser is happy with that quality.
I can keep that volume steady. Could you ask for $45 per QFTD, up from $40, from the 1st?
I will ask today and confirm in writing.

steps.say: Here's what that looks like in practice. This example is a Telegram-style chat with an affiliate manager. Read the first message: the buyer leads with data, one hundred and eighteen qualified F T Ds a month, seventy one percent qualification, under two percent chargebacks, with a sub I D report attached. The manager says the advertiser is happy. Then the buyer asks for a specific number, forty five dollars, up from forty. And the manager agrees to ask and confirm in writing. No threats, no bluff.

steps.h: What a small raise is worth
steps.p: Example: you send 120 qualified FTDs a month at $40 and negotiate $45. That $5 increase adds $600 a month at the same spend, which goes straight to profit.
steps.more: Worked example. Before: 120 × $40 = $4,800. After: 120 × $45 = $5,400. Difference $600 a month, or $7,200 over a year if volume holds. If your profit was $1,200 a month, the raise lifts it by half without touching a single ad. This is why serious operators build relationships with managers and share honest quality data.
steps.say: Small raises add up. In this example, you send one hundred and twenty qualified F T Ds a month at forty dollars, and you negotiate forty five. That five dollar increase adds six hundred dollars a month, the number on screen, at the same spend. It goes straight to profit. If volume holds, that's seven thousand two hundred dollars a year without touching a single ad. That's why serious operators build relationships with managers.

steps.h: Being a partner, not a customer
steps.p: Affiliate managers handle many affiliates. The ones they help first are the ones who are easy to work with and send traffic the advertiser keeps. Be that affiliate.

exam.q: A cohort produces NGR of $4,000, $2,000 and $1,000 over three months. Deal A is $30 CPA on 100 FTDs. Deal B is 40% RevShare. After three months, which earned more?
exam.why: A: 100 × $30 = $3,000. B: $7,000 × 0.40 = $2,800. CPA is ahead after three months.

options: Say Meta only and add Telegram quietly later

exam.why: Undeclared sources can lead to unpaid conversions. Declare what you run and get written approval before adding a new source.

options: Accept but use a different ad account
Refuse and target the legal age or higher, and question working with that network
exam.why: Targeting under the legal age breaks the law and platform policy. A network suggesting it is a red flag.

options: You cannot tell which ad set produced the FTDs, so the rule card cannot be applied per ad set
Ads Manager will reject the link
exam.why: Without sub IDs per campaign, ad set and ad, network conversions cannot be matched, so kill and scale decisions are guesses.

options: No deal until you have more cash
exam.why: CPA pays a fixed amount soon after qualification, so it fits tight cash flow and unknown player quality.

exam.q: Your network scrubs 40% of FTDs this month with no reason. Last month it was 10%. What is the best first step?
options: Stop all traffic and post about it publicly
Send your own sub ID data and ask for the scrub reasons in writing within the hold period
Increase volume to make up the difference
exam.why: Reconcile with your own records and ask for reasons while you can still dispute. Then decide based on the answer.

options: Run it, the network made it
Run it only in Tier 3 geos
Do not run it as is; ask for an honest lander with a chance-to-win message and real rules
exam.why: It claims a win and uses fake urgency, which is misleading. Run only honest landers with published rules.
